turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Doctor. I guess... well, they told me I had to come in. It's my talking. They say my talking gets all mixed up. 

See, I work as a cleaner, a janitor, mostly the night shifts, and I try to explain things to people, just trying to get my point across, but... well, I try to explain about the keys. I have this huge ring of them for the building, all these heavy brass and silver keys clinking around against my leg, and I'll be explaining that, and then I start talking about the jail, because of the locks and the bars and being trapped, you know? It just makes sense to bring it up right then. And then I move on to the prayer rug, the one with the woven patterns and the tassels, and then the chess pieces—the knights and the bishops and how they move across the board—because it's all part of the exact same thing I'm trying to say. 

But people... they just stare at me. My supervisor, my sister, they just get this look on their face. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying at all. They say my words are just a big tangled mess, even though I'm just trying to explain the whole situation to them, from the keys right down to the chess board. I don't feel mixed up, but everyone else says they can't understand a lick of it. So, I guess that's why I'm sitting here today.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech jumping loosely between unrelated topics (keys, jail, prayer rug, chess pieces) and reports that others cannot follow what they are saying, indicating disorganized thinking and speech (loose associations).
